newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Malaysia cocoa bean exports seen continuing lower.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia cocoa bean exports seen continuing lower.

text.p: Falling area and a rise in domestic processing capacity has eaten into Malaysia's cocoa bean exports, and the trend is expected to continue, Dutch agri-bank Rabobank said in a study.
The sector faced mounting competition from less labour-intensive crops such as palm oil, it said in a report on the country's agribusiness.
The future of cocoa growing largely depended on developments in the local processing industry, which Rabobank said was progressing well.
But there was a danger that quality processing might move abroad to the country of consumption and for this reason Malaysia had to look to Asia to sell chocolate products.

"Malaysia companies...will shift the location of their operations from their home base to the country of consumption. The local production which survives will only supply the home market and the markets in neighbouring countries," it said.

Rabobank said the Asian market did not have a taste preference for African cocoa-based chocolate and its per capita consumption was low. The region could become the driving force behind the Malaysian chocolate industry.

Malaysian bean exports were increasingly dependent on China, currently the country's second largest buyer, taking around 20 percent of the total. Some of this is due to the establishment of joint grinding facilities in China.
Around 37 percent of exports went to Singapore, but much was then re-exported.
Domestic consumption of cocoa was increasing, spurred on by increases in disposable income and generally low cocoa prices.
Sales were growing at between eight and 10 percent a year.
But per capita consumption remained low at 300-400 grammes compared with, for example, Switzerland's 11 kg.
